## 12. Weighted and generalized least squares encode different reasons for weighting

Weighted least squares minimizes

$$
\sum_i w_i(y_i-x_i^T\beta)^2.
$$

If independent errors have known variances \(\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon_i\mid X)=\sigma_i^2\), choosing \(w_i=1/\sigma_i^2\) gives more influence to precise observations. More generally, if \(\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon\mid X)=\Sigma\), generalized least squares minimizes

$$
(y-X\beta)^T\Sigma^{-1}(y-X\beta).
$$

Whitening by a matrix \(L\) with \(L^TL=\Sigma^{-1}\) turns this into ordinary least squares on \(Ly\) and \(LX\).

Do not confuse precision weights with sampling or inverse-propensity weights. Precision weighting changes efficiency for a conditional model. Sampling weights change which population the estimating equation represents. Frequency weights describe replicated cases. Software may use the same argument name for all three while their estimands and valid uncertainty differ.

**Worked example — benchmark aggregation.** Suppose task-level score estimates have different Monte Carlo variances. Inverse-variance weighting estimates a precision-weighted task effect, not the average effect over a deployment task distribution. If deployment weights are specified, use those for the estimand and propagate each task's uncertainty separately.

## 13. A generalized linear model has three moving parts

A generalized linear model (GLM) specifies:

1. an exponential-family conditional distribution for \(Y_i\mid x_i\);
2. a linear predictor \(\eta_i=x_i^T\beta\);
3. a link \(g\) connecting the conditional mean \(\mu_i=E[Y_i\mid x_i]\) to the predictor:

$$
g(\mu_i)=\eta_i.
$$

![A GLM maps predictors through a linear predictor and inverse link to a conditional outcome distribution.](../assets/glm-link-mean.svg)

For a one-parameter exponential family with dispersion \(\phi\), a common representation is

$$
p(y\mid\theta,\phi)
=\exp\left(
\frac{y\theta-b(\theta)}{a(\phi)}+c(y,\phi)
\right).
$$

Then

$$
E[Y]=b'(\theta),
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(Y)=b''(\theta)a(\phi).
$$

The **canonical link** sets the natural parameter \(\theta\) equal to \(x^T\beta\). Identity is canonical for Gaussian means, logit for Bernoulli means, and log for Poisson means. Noncanonical links are allowed when scientific interpretation or constraints favor them.

| Outcome | Mean range | Common link | Conditional variance |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Gaussian | \(\mathbb R\) | identity | \(\sigma^2\) |
| Bernoulli | \((0,1)\) | logit | \(\mu(1-\mu)\) |
| Poisson | \((0,\infty)\) | log | \(\mu\) |

The link does not transform observed outcomes into Gaussian data. It transforms the modeled mean. A log link does not mean “take logs and run OLS”; zeros remain valid Poisson outcomes and the variance model remains different.

**Worked example — choosing all three parts.** For whether an evaluation item passes, choose a Bernoulli outcome, linear predictor containing system and task features, and logit link. For failures counted over unequal accelerator-hours, choose a Poisson or overdispersed count family, a predictor with hardware features, a log link, and log exposure as an offset. Changing only the link does not turn a binary outcome into a count model.

## 14. Logistic regression models log odds and Bernoulli information

For \(Y_i\in\{0,1\}\), logistic regression sets

$$
p_i=P(Y_i=1\mid x_i)=\sigma(x_i^T\beta),
\qquad
\log\frac{p_i}{1-p_i}=x_i^T\beta.
$$

The log likelihood is

$$
\ell(\beta)=\sum_i\left[y_i\eta_i-\log(1+e^{\eta_i})\right],
\qquad \eta_i=x_i^T\beta.
$$

Its score and observed information are

$$
\nabla\ell=X^T(y-p),
\qquad
-\nabla^2\ell=X^TWX,
$$

where \(W_{ii}=p_i(1-p_i)\). The information vanishes near probabilities zero and one: labels there change the fitted boundary less than uncertain cases with similar predictor geometry.

Exponentiating \(\beta_j\) gives the conditional **odds ratio** for a one-unit predictor increase, holding represented covariates fixed. It is not a risk ratio and not a constant probability difference. The probability change depends on the starting probability:

$$
\frac{\partial p}{\partial x_j}=\beta_jp(1-p).
$$

**Worked example — the same odds ratio, different probability changes.** If \(\beta_j=\log2\), the odds double. Starting at \(p=0.5\), probability becomes \(2/3\), a 0.167 increase. Starting at \(p=0.01\), it becomes about 0.0198, an increase below 0.01.

Evaluate probabilistic predictions with proper losses and calibration, not only a thresholded accuracy. Case-control or outcome-dependent sampling can preserve some slope information while changing the intercept and deployment probabilities; sampling design must be reflected in fitting and recalibration.

## 15. Bradley–Terry turns pairwise preferences into a logistic model

Logistic regression models a binary outcome given covariates. Replace "did the event occur" with "did item \(i\) beat item \(j\)" and the same machinery becomes the standard model for preference data — the likelihood behind reward models, arena leaderboards, and every head-to-head evaluation in AI research.

**The model.** Give each item a latent strength \(\theta_i\). The Bradley–Terry model says

$$
P(i\succ j)=\frac{e^{\theta_i}}{e^{\theta_i}+e^{\theta_j}}
=\sigma(\theta_i-\theta_j),
$$

with \(\sigma\) the logistic function. Read that second form carefully: **Bradley–Terry is logistic regression with a design matrix of \(+1\), \(-1\), and zeros.** For a comparison between \(i\) and \(j\), the covariate vector has \(+1\) in position \(i\), \(-1\) in position \(j\), and zeros elsewhere; the coefficient vector is \(\theta\). Everything in the previous section applies unchanged: the log-odds are linear, the Bernoulli information is \(\sigma(1-\sigma)\), and fitting is iteratively reweighted least squares.

**Identifiability.** Only differences \(\theta_i-\theta_j\) enter the likelihood, so \(\theta\) and \(\theta+c\mathbf1\) give identical probabilities. The parameter is identified only up to an additive constant, exactly the non-identifiability discussed for sufficiency earlier in this lesson. Fix it by pinning one item to zero or by constraining \(\sum_i\theta_i=0\). Reporting "model A scored 1183" is meaningless without stating the constraint and the reference set.

**Worked example.** Suppose \(\hat\theta_A-\hat\theta_B=0.7\). Then

$$
P(A\succ B)=\sigma(0.7)=\frac1{1+e^{-0.7}}\approx0.668 .
$$

A strength difference of \(0.7\) log-odds is a \(67\%\) win rate, not a \(70\%\) one — the logistic link is not the identity, and reading coefficient differences as probabilities is a common error.

**Information and design.** From the logistic Fisher information, a comparison between \(i\) and \(j\) contributes \(\sigma(1-\sigma)\) to the information about \(\theta_i-\theta_j\), which is maximized at \(\sigma=1/2\) — that is, when the two items are **evenly matched**. Comparisons between a strong and a hopeless item carry almost no information. This is the statistical justification for adaptive matchmaking in evaluation arenas, and it is also the reason a leaderboard built from random pairings is far less efficient than its sample size suggests.

**Ties and multiple comparisons.** Basic Bradley–Terry has no tie category; extensions (Davidson, or an ordinal model) add one. Dropping ties instead is a selection decision and biases strengths toward whichever items tie less often.

**Where it breaks, and this matters for AI evaluation.**

- **Non-transitivity.** The model forces a total order. If A beats B, B beats C, and C beats A systematically, no \(\theta\) fits, and the estimate will average the cycle away without warning. Test by comparing observed win rates against fitted ones on triads.
- **Rater dependence.** Multiple judgments from one rater, or one prompt, are clustered. Standard errors must use cluster-robust or bootstrap-by-rater methods, exactly as established earlier in this lesson; treating each comparison as independent understates uncertainty, often by a large factor.
- **Position and verbosity bias.** If judges prefer the first-shown or longer response, that effect is a covariate, not noise. Add it to the design matrix and estimate it — the model already accommodates extra columns.
- **Nonstationary populations.** Strengths estimated against one opponent pool do not transfer to another. A rating is relative to the field.

The practical recommendation: report strengths with a stated constraint, cluster-robust intervals, an explicit tie policy, and a non-transitivity check. A leaderboard without those is a point estimate with unknown uncertainty.

## 16. Poisson regression models rates through exposure

For a count \(Y_i\geq0\), Poisson regression uses

$$
Y_i\mid x_i\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(\mu_i),
\qquad
\log\mu_i=x_i^T\beta.
$$

If observations have exposures \(t_i\), model a rate by including a fixed **offset**:

$$
\log\mu_i=\log t_i+x_i^T\beta.
$$

The offset coefficient is fixed at one. Exponentiating \(\beta_j\) gives a multiplicative rate ratio.

The Poisson variance equals its mean. Real count data often show **overdispersion** from heterogeneity, clustering, excess zeros, or dependence. The Pearson dispersion diagnostic

$$
\hat\phi=\frac1{n-p}\sum_i\frac{(y_i-\hat\mu_i)^2}{\hat\mu_i}
$$

substantially above one signals that model-based Poisson uncertainty is too small. Quasi-Poisson scaling, negative-binomial models, cluster-robust covariance, random effects, or a better mean model address different causes; choose by mechanism rather than by a single diagnostic number.

**Worked example — failures per accelerator-hour.** A machine observed for 100 hours and one observed for 10 hours should not be compared as raw counts. With \(\log t_i\) as an offset, a coefficient for hardware type compares failure rates at equal exposure. Treating exposure as an ordinary learned predictor wrongly estimates whether counts scale proportionally with observed time.

## 17. GLM fitting is repeated local weighted least squares

For canonical GLMs, log likelihood is concave in \(\beta\) when the design is well behaved. Newton's update is

$$
\beta_{\text{new}}
=\beta_{\text{old}}
+(X^TWX)^{-1}X^T(y-\mu).
$$

It can be written as **iteratively reweighted least squares** (IRLS): construct a working response \(z\) by locally linearizing the link, then solve weighted least squares with weights determined by current fitted variance and link derivative. Recompute and repeat.

Numerical safeguards still matter:

- compute logistic loss with stable softplus identities;
- solve linear systems rather than invert \(X^TWX\);
- use line search or trust-region damping when Newton steps are too aggressive;
- standardize poorly scaled predictors for optimization while preserving interpretable transformations;
- check rank, convergence, gradient size, and coefficient path.

In completely separated logistic data, likelihood approaches its supremum as some coefficient norms diverge. The Hessian can be positive semidefinite while no finite MLE exists. Penalization, weakly informative priors, or bias-reduced likelihood can yield finite estimates, but the separation itself should be reported.

**Worked example — rare safety failures.** If one feature perfectly separates all observed failures from successes, an optimizer may return increasingly large coefficients and tiny fitted loss. This is not strong finite evidence for a precisely known effect. It is a boundary estimate driven by limited overlap. Inspect feature-label tables, coefficient paths, and held-out behavior.

## 18. Deviance and residuals compare fitted distributions

For a fitted GLM, the **saturated model** gives each observation enough freedom to reproduce its outcome. Deviance compares fitted log likelihood with saturated log likelihood:

$$
D=2\left(\ell_{\mathrm{sat}}-\ell_{\mathrm{fit}}\right).
$$

For Poisson observations,

$$
D=2\sum_i
\left[y_i\log\frac{y_i}{\hat\mu_i}-(y_i-\hat\mu_i)\right],
$$

with the \(y_i\log(y_i/\hat\mu_i)\) term defined as zero when \(y_i=0\). Deviance residuals assign signed square roots of observation contributions. Pearson residuals scale \(y_i-\hat\mu_i\) by modeled standard deviation.

For nested regular models, a deviance difference is a likelihood-ratio statistic and is often approximately chi-squared with degrees of freedom equal to the parameter-count difference. Boundaries, small samples, adaptive model selection, separation, and misspecification can invalidate that calibration.

Predictive model comparison asks a different question. Cross-validated log loss estimates out-of-sample predictive performance for a specified split distribution. In-sample deviance rewards flexibility and should not be mistaken for deployment evidence.

**Worked example — omitted interaction.** A logistic model fits language and model version as additive effects. Deviance residuals show opposite version errors across languages. Adding a prespecified language-by-version interaction tests whether the version contrast changes by language. If the pattern was discovered by searching hundreds of slices, confirmation needs fresh data or selection-aware inference.

## 19. Mixed-effects models represent group variation and partial pooling

Rows in AI research are often nested: outputs within prompts, prompts within tasks, users within organizations, or checkpoints within training runs. A random-intercept model is

$$
y_{ij}=x_{ij}^T\beta+b_j+\varepsilon_{ij},
\qquad
b_j\sim\mathcal N(0,\tau^2),
\qquad
\varepsilon_{ij}\sim\mathcal N(0,\sigma^2).
$$

\(\beta\) describes population-level fixed effects; \(b_j\) describes modeled group deviations. Marginally, two rows in the same group have covariance \(\tau^2\), so the model represents dependence rather than pretending rows are independent.

For a group mean \(\bar y_j\) with \(n_j\) observations and a known population mean \(\mu\), the normal-normal posterior or empirical-Bayes predictor has the form

$$
\tilde\mu_j
=w_j\bar y_j+(1-w_j)\mu,
\qquad
w_j=\frac{\tau^2}{\tau^2+\sigma^2/n_j}.
$$

Small or noisy groups shrink more toward the population; large precise groups shrink less.

![Partial pooling shrinks noisy group estimates more strongly than precise group estimates.](../assets/partial-pooling.svg)

**No pooling** fits unrelated group parameters and can overreact to tiny groups. **Complete pooling** erases heterogeneity. **Partial pooling** shares information through an estimated population distribution. Random slopes allow treatment or predictor effects to vary across groups, but estimating their covariance needs enough independent groups.

Maximum likelihood estimates fixed effects and variance components jointly. Restricted maximum likelihood adjusts Gaussian variance-component estimation for fitted fixed effects. Bayesian models place priors on every level and propagate variance-component uncertainty. With few groups, asymptotic standard errors and estimated heterogeneity can be unstable under either approach.

**Worked example — benchmark tasks.** A system effect may vary by task. Treating 5,000 examples as independent understates new-task uncertainty; fitting 20 unrelated effects makes small tasks erratic. A random-slope model estimates the average system effect, between-task variation, and partially pooled task effects. It still requires the sampled tasks to represent the target task population.

> **Practice — Foundation:** Compute \(w_j\) when \(\tau^2=1\), \(\sigma^2=4\), and \(n_j=1,4,100\).
>
> **Practice — Core:** Derive the covariance between two observations in the same random-intercept group and the resulting intraclass correlation.
>
> **Practice — Stretch:** Design a crossed random-effects model for model outputs scored by both prompts and raters, stating the population represented by each random factor.

## 20. A disciplined regression workflow for AI research

### Before fitting

1. Define the population, unit, outcome, intervention or predictor, and target contrast.
2. Draw the dependence structure: task, prompt, user, rater, run, checkpoint, and time.
3. Decide whether the goal is description, prediction, or causal estimation.
4. Specify functional form, interactions, exposure, and link before viewing every result.
5. Reserve data for selection, calibration, and final evaluation at the appropriate group and time level.

### During fitting

1. Inspect support and overlap rather than only marginal histograms.
2. use stable likelihood calculations and rank-aware solvers;
3. record preprocessing, coding, weights, offsets, regularization, and convergence;
4. model or preserve dependence;
5. diagnose mean form, variance, tails, leverage, separation, overdispersion, and group heterogeneity separately.

### After fitting

1. Report effects on an interpretable scale with uncertainty.
2. distinguish conditional coefficients, marginal predictions, and causal effects;
3. compare against held-out data using proper predictive scores and target-weighted summaries;
4. run sensitivity analyses for coding, functional form, clusters, influential groups, missingness, and shift;
5. preserve residual and subgroup diagnostics without turning exploratory discoveries into confirmatory claims.

**Worked example — comparing agent versions.** Use a paired task design and model success with version, task characteristics, and prespecified interactions. Add task random effects and, if enough tasks exist, a random version slope. Report the population-average probability difference using marginal predictions, not only a conditional odds ratio. Validate calibration and performance on later tasks, and keep adaptive failure discovery separate from confirmation.

> **Practice — Foundation:** Label five statements as descriptive, predictive, or causal regression goals.
>
> **Practice — Core:** Write a complete regression specification for repeated binary judgments nested within prompts and raters.
>
> **Practice — Stretch:** Audit a model-comparison paper whose rows are completions but whose claimed population is tasks; redesign its model, uncertainty, and split.

## 21. Runnable labs

This chapter has three coding exercises. Each opens as a separate tab in the lesson's right-hand Python workspace.

### Lab A — simple OLS and slope uncertainty

Implement **simple_ols** in [labs/exercises.py](../../labs/exercises.py). Given finite predictor and outcome iterables, return:

1. fitted intercept;
2. fitted slope;
3. residual standard error using \(n-2\) degrees of freedom;
4. conventional homoskedastic slope standard error.

Run:

~~~text
python -m labs.checks simple-ols
~~~

The checks cover exact lines, noisy data, translation and scaling behavior, generators, input preservation, degenerate predictors, and invalid observations.

### Lab B — stable logistic loss and gradient

Implement **logistic_loss_gradient** in [labs/exercises.py](../../labs/exercises.py). Given a finite rectangular design matrix, binary outcomes, and coefficients, return the mean Bernoulli negative log likelihood and its gradient.

Run:

~~~text
python -m labs.checks logistic-gradient
~~~

The checks cover ordinary and extreme logits, numerical gradients, generators, input preservation, shape failures, and invalid binary labels.

### Lab C — normal-normal partial pooling

Implement **partial_pooling_means** in [labs/exercises.py](../../labs/exercises.py). Given group means, positive group sizes, known within-group variance, a population mean, and between-group variance, return pooled group means and their data weights \(w_j\).

Run:

~~~text
python -m labs.checks partial-pooling
~~~

The checks cover no heterogeneity, noiseless observations, unequal group sizes, translation, generators, input preservation, and invalid variance or sample-size inputs.

### Guided experiment

1. Verify that Bernoulli likelihoods are identical for sequences with the same sufficient count, then add time drift and show the equivalence disappears.
2. Numerically differentiate Bernoulli and Poisson log-partition functions to recover means and variances.
3. Simulate OLS under Gaussian, heavy-tailed, heteroskedastic, and clustered errors; compare model-based, HC, and cluster-robust coverage.
4. Fit the same categorical comparison as a difference in means, regression, and ANOVA contrast.
5. Trace logistic Newton steps as separation increases and compare penalized fits.
6. Simulate Poisson rates with unequal exposure, then add latent rate heterogeneity and diagnose overdispersion.
7. Vary group sizes and variance ratios to visualize partial-pooling weights and new-group predictive uncertainty.

## 22. Derivations to own

1. Prove Bernoulli sufficiency both by factorization and by conditional distribution.
2. Apply the likelihood-ratio criterion for minimal sufficiency.
3. Derive sufficient statistics for Gaussian data with unknown mean and variance.
4. Put Bernoulli, Poisson, categorical, and fixed-variance Gaussian distributions in natural exponential-family form.
5. Derive \(\nabla A(\eta)=E[T]\) and \(\nabla^2A(\eta)=\operatorname{Cov}(T)\).
6. Derive exponential-family MLE moment matching.
7. Prove the Rao–Blackwell variance inequality with total variance.
8. Derive OLS normal equations, projection, and coefficient covariance.
9. Derive \(t\)- and \(F\)-statistics for linear contrasts under Gaussian errors.
10. Derive HC and cluster-sandwich covariance estimators from score contributions.
11. Show GLS is OLS after whitening.
12. Derive logistic and Poisson scores and Hessians.
13. Derive IRLS from a second-order likelihood approximation.
14. Derive Poisson deviance and its zero-count convention.
15. Derive normal-normal partial pooling and the random-intercept intraclass correlation.

## 23. End-of-unit practice (graded)

**Foundation — problems 1–7.** Recognize likelihood structure and compute direct regression quantities.

1. **Factorization.** Identify sufficient statistics in Bernoulli, Poisson, and fixed-variance Gaussian samples.
2. **Natural form.** Convert four common distributions into exponential-family notation.
3. **Partition derivatives.** Recover a Bernoulli or Poisson mean and variance from \(A\).
4. **Simple OLS.** Calculate intercept, slope, residual variance, and slope standard error by hand.
5. **Indicators.** Encode a four-level category and interpret coefficients under two reference choices.
6. **Logistic effects.** Convert log odds to probabilities and compare odds ratios with risk differences.
7. **Poisson exposure.** Fit rate comparisons using offsets and interpret rate ratios.

**Core — problems 8–15.** Connect estimation, diagnostics, and uncertainty.

8. **Minimal sufficiency.** Use likelihood ratios to partition a finite sample space into minimal-sufficient equivalence classes.
9. **Rao–Blackwell.** Improve an unbiased estimator by conditioning on a sufficient statistic and compare exact variances.
10. **ANOVA as regression.** Construct a factorial design matrix, test main and interaction contrasts, and recover cell means.
11. **Heteroskedasticity.** Simulate a correct linear mean with changing variance and compare conventional with HC coverage.
12. **Clusters.** Compare row-wise, cluster-robust, and cluster-mean uncertainty as intraclass correlation changes.
13. **GLS.** Build a correlated covariance matrix, whiten the data, and verify the GLS solution.
14. **Logistic optimization.** Implement damped Newton or IRLS and test it against finite-difference gradients.
15. **Count diagnostics.** Separate omitted mean structure, overdispersion, excess zeros, and exposure mistakes.

**Stretch — problems 16–24.** Analyze research-scale models and assumption failures.

16. **Sufficiency under drift.** Construct samples with identical classical sufficient statistics but different evidence under a nonstationary alternative.
17. **Curved family.** Restrict a multiparameter exponential family to a nonlinear parameter curve and study identifiability and moment matching.
18. **Separation.** Characterize a separating direction, demonstrate coefficient divergence, and compare three remedies.
19. **Post-selection inference.** Search many interactions, select the best, and measure the false confidence of its naive interval.
20. **Target mismatch.** Show how precision, sampling, and frequency weights answer different estimands on the same rows.
21. **Rare outcomes.** Compare logistic, Poisson-rate, and case-control analyses under severe imbalance and deployment shift.
22. **Crossed effects.** Model outputs nested simultaneously within tasks, prompts, raters, and training runs; identify which variance components support each claim.
23. **Partial pooling failure.** Simulate multimodal group effects that violate a single Gaussian random-effects distribution and assess population and subgroup consequences.
24. **Complete AI study.** Design a regression analysis whose sampling frame, link, dependence model, uncertainty, diagnostics, multiplicity control, and held-out evaluation all match one deployment claim.

<details><summary>Worked solution sketches</summary>

1. Factor parameter-dependent terms. Bernoulli and Poisson use sums; fixed-variance Gaussian location uses \(\sum y_i\).
2. Choose natural parameters so the exponent is linear in \(T(y)\); whatever normalizes the density enters \(A\), while parameter-free terms enter \(h\).
3. Differentiate \(A\). The first derivative is the mean statistic and the second is its variance because differentiation tilts the normalized density.
4. Center \(x\) and \(y\): \(\hat\beta_1=S_{xy}/S_{xx}\), \(\hat\beta_0=\bar y-\hat\beta_1\bar x\), \(s^2=\operatorname{RSS}/(n-2)\), and \(\operatorname{SE}(\hat\beta_1)=s/\sqrt{S_{xx}}\).
5. Use one fewer indicator than levels with an intercept. Reference changes reparameterize the same fitted cell means.
6. Add coefficients on the log-odds scale, apply sigmoid, and compare probability differences at several baselines. Odds and risk are different denominators.
7. Include log exposure with coefficient fixed at one. Exponentiated learned coefficients compare rates, not raw expected counts.
8. Two samples belong together exactly when their likelihood ratio is parameter-free. The resulting equivalence-class label is minimal sufficient.
9. Compute \(E[U\mid T]\). Total variance shows removal of \(E[\operatorname{Var}(U\mid T)]\), while iterated expectation preserves unbiasedness.
10. Indicator and interaction columns span the cell-mean model. Main-effect interpretation depends on coding and interactions; joint contrasts recover reference-invariant questions.
11. OLS point estimates target the linear conditional mean, but constant-variance standard errors misweight residual information. HC covariance restores large-sample coverage when independent-unit assumptions hold.
12. Positive within-cluster covariance makes row-wise information grow too quickly. Cluster scores preserve shared shocks; with few clusters, use cautious finite-sample or design-based methods.
13. Find \(L\) with \(L^TL=\Sigma^{-1}\), transform \(X,y\), and solve OLS. Both objectives and normal equations coincide.
14. Use \(X^T(p-y)/n\) for loss gradient and \(X^TWX/n\) for its Hessian. Stable softplus prevents overflow; damping ensures actual descent.
15. Plot residuals against fitted means and predictors, inspect zeros and exposure, and use replication or a mechanism-specific model. One dispersion number cannot locate the cause.
16. Reorder equal counts so successes occur early versus late. An iid Bernoulli likelihood ties them; a trend model does not.
17. A nonlinear restriction can make sufficient-statistic dimension exceed parameter dimension and prevent arbitrary moment matching. Analyze the restricted image in mean-parameter space.
18. A direction classifying every observation lets margins grow without likelihood penalty. Penalization, informative priors, or bias reduction make estimates finite but encode additional structure.
19. The selected maximum coefficient has a truncated, winner-biased distribution. Repeat the entire search in resampling or use fresh confirmation data.
20. Precision weights optimize variance, sampling weights reconstruct a population, and frequency weights duplicate cases. Write each estimating equation and read off its target.
21. Separate sampling prevalence from conditional slopes, use offsets for person-time when appropriate, and recalibrate probabilities under changed prevalence.
22. Introduce crossed random intercepts and justified slopes. New-task claims need task variation; new-run claims need run variation; rater uncertainty needs sampled raters.
23. A single Gaussian distribution may overshrink distinct modes toward an implausible center. Compare mixture or structured group models and validate new-group prediction.
24. A complete answer fixes the estimand first, then aligns design matrix, link, weights, grouping, solver, standard error, diagnostic plan, selection control, and final split with it.

</details>

## Mastery check

Given an unfamiliar regression claim, reconstruct the conditional probability model; identify its sufficient statistics and exponential-family structure where present; derive its score, information, and estimand; fit it stably; choose uncertainty matching heteroskedasticity and dependence; interpret effects on appropriate conditional and marginal scales; diagnose functional-form, leverage, separation, overdispersion, and selection failures; and decide whether no pooling, complete pooling, or partial pooling matches the population being studied.

The next advanced statistics unit should develop predictive uncertainty, calibration, proper scoring rules, and conformal prediction. Those ideas use GLM probabilities as a concrete starting point while extending guarantees beyond a single parametric outcome model.

# High-dimensional probability, random vectors, and projections

Every intuition you own about probability was built in one, two, or three dimensions. Embeddings live in 768. Hidden states live in 4096. Parameter vectors live in \(10^{11}\). The claim of this unit is not that high dimensions are *harder*; it is that they are **different in kind**, and that the differences are precise, provable, and directly responsible for facts you already use — why attention divides by \(\sqrt{d_k}\), why initialization scales as \(1/\sqrt{\text{fan\_in}}\), why cosine similarity behaves the way it does, and why a covariance estimated from a few thousand samples is badly wrong in a way that is not obvious from the average.

The unifying phenomenon is **concentration of measure**: as dimension grows, well-behaved functions of a random vector stop being random. Averages concentrate — that was the law of large numbers in [repeated samples and limit theorems](05-limit-theorems-monte-carlo.md). Here, *geometry itself* concentrates.

## 0. Prerequisite check

You should be able to state the weak law and Chebyshev's inequality, compute the mean and variance of a sum of independent variables, recognize \(\chi^2\) as a sum of squared standard normals, and read \(\lVert\cdot\rVert\) and eigenvalues of a symmetric matrix. If the last item is uncertain, revisit [eigenvalues and invariant subspaces](../02-linear-algebra/04-eigenvalues-invariant-subspaces.md) first.

## 1. Two dimensions lie to you

Draw \(x\sim\mathcal N(0,I_d)\): each coordinate is an independent standard normal. Ask a simple question — *where is this vector?*

In \(d=1\), the density peaks at the origin, so the typical point is near zero. That intuition is correct in \(d=1\), survives in \(d=2\), and is **false** in \(d=100\).

The density is still maximal at the origin. But the *volume* available at radius \(r\) grows like \(r^{d-1}\), and the product of a shrinking density with an exploding volume concentrates sharply away from zero. The mass is not where the density is highest. This is the first and most important correction to low-dimensional intuition: **in high dimensions, typical and most-likely are different places.**

Three consequences follow, and the next three sections prove each one.

1. Almost every sample has nearly the same norm, \(\lVert x\rVert\approx\sqrt d\).
2. Almost every pair of samples is nearly orthogonal.
3. Almost all the mass sits in a thin shell, not in the interior and not in any corner.

## 2. The norm concentrates: \(\lVert x\rVert\approx\sqrt d\)

Let \(x\sim\mathcal N(0,I_d)\). Then \(\lVert x\rVert^2=\sum_{i=1}^dx_i^2\) is a sum of \(d\) independent terms, each with

$$
E[x_i^2]=1,
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(x_i^2)=E[x_i^4]-1=3-1=2 .
$$

So by linearity and independence,

$$
E\bigl[\lVert x\rVert^2\bigr]=d,
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}\bigl(\lVert x\rVert^2\bigr)=2d .
$$

This is already the whole story. The *mean* grows like \(d\) while the *standard deviation* grows only like \(\sqrt{2d}\), so the **relative** fluctuation is

$$
\frac{\operatorname{sd}(\lVert x\rVert^2)}{E[\lVert x\rVert^2]}
=\frac{\sqrt{2d}}d
=\sqrt{\frac2d}
\;\longrightarrow\;0 .
$$

Chebyshev's inequality converts this into a bound: for any \(t>0\),

$$
P\left(\left|\frac{\lVert x\rVert^2}d-1\right|\ge t\right)
\le\frac{2}{dt^2}.
$$

**Worked example — \(d=4096\).** The relative standard deviation of \(\lVert x\rVert^2\) is \(\sqrt{2/4096}\approx0.022\). Taking square roots, \(\lVert x\rVert\) sits within about \(1\%\) of \(\sqrt{4096}=64\) for the overwhelming majority of draws. A "random hidden state" is not a vector of unpredictable length. Its length is essentially deterministic; only its *direction* is random.

The Chebyshev bound is weak — it decays like \(1/d\). Because \(x_i^2\) is sub-exponential rather than bounded, Bernstein's inequality (developed in [the concentration section of the limit-theorems lesson](05-limit-theorems-monte-carlo.md)) sharpens it to an exponential ceiling,

$$
P\bigl(\bigl|\lVert x\rVert^2-d\bigr|\ge td\bigr)
\le2\exp\bigl(-c\,d\min(t,t^2)\bigr),
$$

for an absolute constant \(c\). Deviations of fixed relative size become exponentially unlikely **in the dimension**.

> **Practice — Foundation:** Compute \(E[\lVert x\rVert^2]\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(\lVert x\rVert^2)\) for \(x\sim\mathcal N(0,I_{100})\).
>
> **Practice — Core:** Use Chebyshev to bound \(P(\lVert x\rVert^2\ge1.2d)\) at \(d=1000\), then compare with the exponential form above at \(c=1/8\).
>
> **Practice — Stretch:** Repeat the mean/variance computation for \(x\) with iid coordinates of mean zero, variance \(\sigma^2\), and finite fourth moment \(\kappa\sigma^4\). Show the relative fluctuation is \(\sqrt{(\kappa-1)/d}\) and identify which distributions make concentration slower.

## 3. Random directions are nearly orthogonal

Let \(x,y\sim\mathcal N(0,I_d)\) be independent and let \(\theta\) be the angle between them:

$$
\cos\theta=\frac{x^Ty}{\lVert x\rVert\,\lVert y\rVert}.
$$

By rotational invariance of the standard Gaussian we may condition on \(y\) and rotate it to \(e_1\) without changing the distribution of \(\cos\theta\). Then

$$
\cos\theta=\frac{x_1}{\lVert x\rVert}.
$$

Symmetry across coordinates gives \(E[x_i^2/\lVert x\rVert^2]=1/d\) for every \(i\), since the \(d\) terms are exchangeable and sum to one. Therefore

$$
E[\cos\theta]=0,
\qquad
E[\cos^2\theta]=\frac1d,
\qquad
\operatorname{sd}(\cos\theta)=\frac1{\sqrt d}.
$$

**Worked example — \(d=768\).** The typical cosine similarity between two independent random directions is about \(1/\sqrt{768}\approx0.036\). Two random 768-dimensional vectors are, to a very good approximation, perpendicular.

This single fact underwrites a great deal of embedding practice. A cosine similarity of \(0.30\) sounds unimpressive on a \([-1,1]\) scale, but in \(d=768\) it is more than eight standard deviations from the random baseline. **Similarity scores must be read against the high-dimensional null, not against 1.0.** It also explains why very many nearly-orthogonal directions fit in a space of dimension \(d\): the number of unit vectors with pairwise \(|\cos|\le\varepsilon\) grows exponentially in \(d\), which is what allows a model to store far more distinguishable features than it has dimensions.

![In high dimensions almost all the Gaussian mass lies in a thin shell of radius sqrt(d), and independent directions are nearly perpendicular.](../assets/high-dimensional-shell.svg)

> **Practice — Foundation:** Compute the typical \(|\cos\theta|\) between random directions at \(d=64\), \(d=768\), and \(d=4096\).
>
> **Practice — Core:** A retrieval system reports a cosine similarity of \(0.12\) at \(d=1536\). Express this as a number of standard deviations from the random baseline, and say what further evidence you would want before calling it a match.
>
> **Practice — Stretch:** Embeddings are not isotropic in practice: trained representations often have a dominant common direction. Explain how that inflates raw cosine similarities and design a centering correction, stating what the correction assumes.

## 4. The thin shell, and why "corners" are empty

Combining the previous two sections: the norm is essentially \(\sqrt d\) and the direction is uniform. So the Gaussian in high dimensions is, for practical purposes, the **uniform distribution on a sphere of radius \(\sqrt d\)**, smeared over a shell of thickness \(O(1)\).

The same effect shows in the cube. For \(u\) uniform on \([-1,1]^d\),

$$
E[\lVert u\rVert^2]=d\cdot E[u_1^2]=\frac d3,
$$

so \(\lVert u\rVert\approx\sqrt{d/3}\approx0.577\sqrt d\), while the corner \((\pm1,\ldots,\pm1)\) has norm \(\sqrt d\). The corners are a vanishing fraction of the volume; the inscribed ball is also a vanishing fraction. Almost all the volume of a high-dimensional cube is neither near the center nor near the corners.

The practical reading: **uniform sampling in a high-dimensional box does not explore the box.** Random hyperparameter search, random perturbation baselines, and naive "sample a random point in the region" procedures all inherit this. If you need to cover a region, cover it deliberately — see the sampling designs in [sampling design and ML evaluation](10-sampling-design-ml-evaluation.md).

> **Practice — Foundation:** Compute \(E[\lVert u\rVert]\) approximately for \(u\) uniform on \([-1,1]^{300}\).
>
> **Practice — Core:** Estimate the fraction of the volume of \([-1,1]^d\) lying inside the inscribed unit ball at \(d=20\), and explain why rejection sampling with a cube proposal fails in high dimensions.
>
> **Practice — Stretch:** A perturbation study samples uniformly from a norm ball to test robustness. Explain what part of the ball is actually being tested and propose a sampling scheme that probes the interior as well as the shell.

## 5. Johnson–Lindenstrauss: distances survive random projection

If high dimensions are so strange, can we shrink them? Remarkably, yes, and the amount of shrinkage needed does **not** depend on the original dimension.

Let \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times d}\) have iid \(\mathcal N(0,1/m)\) entries. For a fixed vector \(v\),

$$
E\bigl[\lVert Av\rVert^2\bigr]=\lVert v\rVert^2 ,
$$

because each row \(a_j\) satisfies \(E[(a_j^Tv)^2]=\lVert v\rVert^2/m\). So a random projection preserves squared length *in expectation*, for any \(v\), with no assumptions at all.

Concentration turns "in expectation" into "almost surely". Writing \(\lVert Av\rVert^2/\lVert v\rVert^2\) as an average of \(m\) independent squared standard normals — exactly the object of section 2, with \(m\) in place of \(d\) — gives

$$
P\left(\left|\frac{\lVert Av\rVert^2}{\lVert v\rVert^2}-1\right|>\varepsilon\right)
\le2\exp\left(-\frac{m(\varepsilon^2-\varepsilon^3)}4\right).
$$

Now apply this to the \(\binom n2\) difference vectors \(x_i-x_j\) of an \(n\)-point set and take a union bound. The failure probability is at most \(n^2\exp(-m(\varepsilon^2-\varepsilon^3)/4)\), which is below \(1\) as soon as

$$
m\;\gtrsim\;\frac{8\log n}{\varepsilon^2}.
$$

**The Johnson–Lindenstrauss lemma.** Any \(n\) points in \(\mathbb R^d\) can be mapped into \(\mathbb R^m\) with \(m=O(\varepsilon^{-2}\log n)\) so that all pairwise distances are preserved within a factor \(1\pm\varepsilon\).

Read the bound carefully. \(m\) depends on the **number of points** and the accuracy, and **not on \(d\)**. One million points at \(\varepsilon=0.1\) need roughly \(8\log(10^6)/0.01\approx11{,}000\) dimensions regardless of whether they started in \(10^3\) or \(10^6\).

Two honest caveats. The \(\log n\) is unavoidable, so \(\varepsilon=0.01\) costs a hundred times more dimensions than \(\varepsilon=0.1\) — high accuracy is expensive. And JL preserves *distances*, not every downstream quantity: inner products survive via polarization, but rankings near ties, small-margin decisions, and anything depending on low-variance directions can still flip.

> **Practice — Foundation:** Compute the JL target dimension for \(n=10^4\) points at \(\varepsilon=0.2\) and at \(\varepsilon=0.05\).
>
> **Practice — Core:** Show \(E[\lVert Av\rVert^2]=\lVert v\rVert^2\) directly from the entry distribution of \(A\), and identify where independence is used.
>
> **Practice — Stretch:** Distances are preserved, but a nearest-neighbour ranking is a comparison of distances. Construct a configuration where a \(1\pm\varepsilon\) distance guarantee still permits the top-1 neighbour to change, and state the margin condition that prevents it.

## 6. Estimated covariance is not the covariance

Sections 2 through 5 concerned a *single* random vector. Now take \(n\) samples and estimate the covariance:

$$
\hat\Sigma=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nx_ix_i^T .
$$

Every entry of \(\hat\Sigma\) is an average of \(n\) terms, so each entry is individually accurate to \(O(1/\sqrt n)\). But \(\hat\Sigma\) has \(d^2\) entries, and the *matrix* error in operator norm behaves like

$$
\lVert\hat\Sigma-\Sigma\rVert_{\text{op}}
\;\lesssim\;
\lVert\Sigma\rVert\left(\sqrt{\frac dn}+\frac dn\right),
$$

for sub-Gaussian data. The governing quantity is the **aspect ratio** \(d/n\), not \(n\) alone. Accurate covariance estimation requires \(n\gg d\), not merely \(n\) large.

**Marchenko–Pastur.** Make the truth as simple as possible: let \(\Sigma=I_d\) and let \(\gamma=d/n\) be fixed as both grow. The eigenvalues of \(\hat\Sigma\) do **not** converge to \(1\). They spread across

$$
\bigl[(1-\sqrt\gamma)^2,\;(1+\sqrt\gamma)^2\bigr].
$$

**Worked example — \(d=100\), \(n=400\).** Here \(\gamma=1/4\), so the sample eigenvalues fill \([(1-0.5)^2,(1+0.5)^2]=[0.25,\,2.25]\). The true spectrum is a single point at \(1\). With four times as many samples as dimensions, the estimated spectrum spans a factor of nine. The largest sample eigenvalue is biased **up**, the smallest biased **down**, and the "top principal component" of pure isotropic noise looks convincingly dominant.

Three consequences that matter in practice:

- **PCA on modest sample sizes overstates structure.** A scree plot with a visible leading eigenvalue is not evidence of signal until you compare against the Marchenko–Pastur edge for your \(\gamma\).
- **Whitening amplifies noise.** Whitening divides by \(\sqrt{\hat\lambda_i}\); the smallest eigenvalues are precisely the most underestimated, so whitening inflates the noisiest directions. This is the ill-conditioning argument of [SVD and PCA](../02-linear-algebra/05-svd-pca.md) with a statistical cause.
- **Shrinkage is not optional decoration.** Ledoit–Wolf-style estimators pull \(\hat\Sigma\) toward a scaled identity precisely to undo the spreading above.

This section is also the probabilistic half of a claim made in [nonconvex landscapes](../03-optimization/05-nonconvex-landscapes-training-dynamics.md): random symmetric matrices have spread-out, repelling spectra, which is why a randomly encountered critical point in a large model is overwhelmingly a saddle.

> **Practice — Foundation:** Compute the Marchenko–Pastur support for \(\gamma=0.01\), \(\gamma=0.25\), and \(\gamma=1\).
>
> **Practice — Core:** You have \(n=2000\) samples in \(d=512\) dimensions. Give the MP edges and state the smallest eigenvalue you could observe from pure noise. What does this imply about the rank you would select?
>
> **Practice — Stretch:** Design a permutation-based null for a scree plot: shuffle each feature independently across samples, recompute the spectrum, and compare. Explain precisely which null hypothesis this tests and how it differs from the MP prediction.

## 7. Where this already appears in your models

- **Attention scaling.** For \(q,k\) with iid zero-mean, unit-variance entries, \(q^Tk\) is a sum of \(d_k\) independent terms, so \(\operatorname{Var}(q^Tk)=d_k\) and the logits have standard deviation \(\sqrt{d_k}\). Without the \(1/\sqrt{d_k}\) divisor, softmax inputs grow with head dimension and saturate. This is section 2 applied to an inner product — see [causal transformers](../11-llm-systems/01-causal-transformers-training-systems.md).
- **Initialization.** For \(y=Wx\) with \(W\) entries of variance \(\sigma^2\) and \(x\in\mathbb R^{d}\), \(\operatorname{Var}(y_j)=d\sigma^2\operatorname{Var}(x)\). Holding activation scale constant across layers forces \(\sigma^2\propto1/\text{fan\_in}\). Every initialization scheme is a variance-of-a-sum calculation.
- **Embedding similarity.** Cosine baselines are \(1/\sqrt d\), not \(0\), and anisotropy shifts them further.
- **Random projections and hashing.** JL is the guarantee behind random-projection LSH, sketching, and dimensionality reduction before nearest-neighbour search.
- **Covariance-based methods.** Whitening, PCA, Mahalanobis distances, natural-gradient preconditioners and linear probes all estimate a covariance and all inherit section 6's aspect-ratio problem.
- **Noise injection.** A Gaussian perturbation of standard deviation \(\sigma\) per coordinate has total norm \(\approx\sigma\sqrt d\). Reporting "we added noise of size 0.01" is meaningless without the dimension.

## 8. Failure modes

- **Quoting per-coordinate scale as if it were vector scale.** Always convert: per-coordinate \(\sigma\) means norm \(\sigma\sqrt d\).
- **Comparing cosine similarities across different dimensions** without renormalizing by the \(1/\sqrt d\) baseline.
- **Reading a scree plot without a null.** Structure must be judged against the MP edge or a permutation null.
- **Whitening with an ill-conditioned \(\hat\Sigma\)** when \(n\) is not \(\gg d\).
- **Assuming random search explores a box.** It samples the shell.
- **Treating JL as lossless.** Distances are preserved within \(1\pm\varepsilon\); ties, margins, and rankings are not guaranteed.
- **Applying Gaussian intuition to heavy-tailed coordinates.** Concentration slows as the fourth moment grows, and fails entirely without one.

## 9. Runnable lab: random projection distortion

Implement `projection_distortion` in the [learner exercises file](../../labs/exercises.py). Given a list of points, a target dimension \(m\), and a seed, build \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times d}\) with iid \(\mathcal N(0,1/m)\) entries and return the **largest** relative squared-distance distortion over all distinct pairs:

$$
\max_{i<j}\left|\frac{\lVert A(x_i-x_j)\rVert^2}{\lVert x_i-x_j\rVert^2}-1\right| .
$$

Requirements: reject an empty point list, points of differing length, a non-positive target dimension, and any pair of identical points (the distortion is undefined when the denominator is zero). Seed a local `random.Random(seed)` so results are reproducible without disturbing global state.

Then, outside the graded function, study the behaviour:

1. Fix \(n=60\) points in \(d=512\) and sweep \(m\in\{8,32,128,512\}\). Plot the maximum distortion against \(m\) and compare with the \(\varepsilon\approx\sqrt{8\log n/m}\) prediction.
2. Hold \(m\) fixed and increase \(d\) from \(64\) to \(4096\). Confirm the distortion does **not** grow with \(d\).
3. Increase \(n\) at fixed \(m\) and observe the \(\log n\) penalty appear as a slow rise.
4. Replace Gaussian entries with \(\pm1/\sqrt m\) signs. Verify the distortion is comparable and explain why the proof still works.

## 10. Derivations to own

1. \(E[\lVert x\rVert^2]=d\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(\lVert x\rVert^2)=2d\) for \(x\sim\mathcal N(0,I_d)\), including the \(E[x_i^4]=3\) step.
2. \(E[\cos^2\theta]=1/d\) by rotational invariance and exchangeability.
3. \(E[\lVert Av\rVert^2]=\lVert v\rVert^2\) for a \(1/m\)-variance Gaussian projection.
4. The union-bound step from a single-vector concentration bound to the JL lemma, including where \(\binom n2\) enters.
5. Why \(\operatorname{Var}(q^Tk)=d_k\) and therefore why attention divides by \(\sqrt{d_k}\).
6. The variance-propagation argument giving \(\sigma^2\propto1/\text{fan\_in}\).

## 11. End-of-unit practice (graded)

**Foundation**

1. For \(x\sim\mathcal N(0,I_{1024})\), give the mean and standard deviation of \(\lVert x\rVert^2\), and the approximate value of \(\lVert x\rVert\).
2. Give the typical cosine similarity between independent random directions at \(d=1536\).
3. State the Marchenko–Pastur support at \(\gamma=0.09\).

**Core**

4. A team adds Gaussian noise with per-coordinate \(\sigma=0.02\) to a \(4096\)-dimensional activation and reports a "2% perturbation". Compute the actual relative norm change and correct the claim.
5. Derive the JL target dimension for \(n=5\times10^5\), \(\varepsilon=0.1\), and explain why the answer is unchanged if the points live in \(d=10^4\) or \(d=10^7\).
6. Using the aspect-ratio bound, state how many samples are needed to estimate a \(d=768\) covariance to \(10\%\) operator-norm accuracy, and comment on whether typical probing datasets meet it.
7. Show that the \(\pm1\) sign projection has the same first two moments as the Gaussian projection, and explain the practical advantage.

**Stretch**

8. A linear probe on \(d=4096\) features trained with \(n=2000\) examples reports 91% accuracy. Using section 6, explain why the probe's *weights* may be meaningless even if its *accuracy* is real, and design a check that separates the two claims.
9. Retrieval quality drops when embeddings are projected from 1536 to 256 dimensions, even though measured distance distortion is under 5%. Give three mechanisms consistent with both observations and one experiment that discriminates among them.
10. Construct a distribution on \(\mathbb R^d\) with iid coordinates for which the norm does **not** concentrate at the usual rate, state which moment assumption fails, and say what this implies for JL applied to such data.

<details><summary>Solution sketches</summary>

1. Mean \(1024\), standard deviation \(\sqrt{2048}\approx45.3\), so \(\lVert x\rVert\approx32\) within roughly \(0.7\%\).
2. \(1/\sqrt{1536}\approx0.0255\).
3. \(\sqrt\gamma=0.3\), so \([0.49,1.69]\).
4. The norm change is \(\sigma\sqrt d=0.02\times64=1.28\), while a typical activation norm is itself \(\approx\sqrt d\) times its per-coordinate scale; the relative change is \(\sigma\) divided by the per-coordinate activation scale, so the "2%" claim is only correct if the activations have unit per-coordinate scale. State the per-coordinate scale explicitly or report the ratio of norms.
5. \(m\approx8\log(5\times10^5)/0.01\approx10{,}500\). The bound involves only \(n\) and \(\varepsilon\); \(d\) never enters because the concentration statement is about the \(m\)-dimensional image, not the domain.
6. Requiring \(\sqrt{d/n}\approx0.1\) gives \(n\approx100d\approx76{,}800\). Probing sets of a few thousand examples are far short, so probe covariance structure is unreliable even when probe accuracy is not.
7. Each entry has mean zero and variance \(1/m\), and the concentration proof needs only sub-Gaussianity, which bounded entries satisfy. The advantage is cheaper generation, cheaper multiplication, and less memory.
8. Accuracy depends on the fitted function, which can be stable even when the parameterization is not. With \(d/n>1\) the feature covariance is singular, so the weight vector is not identified: many weight vectors give identical predictions. Check by refitting on bootstrap resamples and reporting the variability of weights versus the variability of accuracy.
9. Possibilities: low-variance but task-relevant directions were destroyed; the distance guarantee holds on average but fails on the small-margin pairs that determine top-\(k\) ranking; anisotropy means the projection interacts with a dominant common direction. Discriminate with a margin analysis of the affected queries, a per-pair distortion histogram restricted to true neighbours, and a centered-embedding rerun.
10. Coordinates with infinite fourth moment, for instance a Student-\(t\) with 3 degrees of freedom: the variance of \(\lVert x\rVert^2\) is infinite, the relative fluctuation does not shrink like \(\sqrt{2/d}\), and JL's exponential bound no longer applies, though weaker statements can survive.

</details>

## Mastery check

Derive the norm and angle concentration results without notes; convert freely between per-coordinate and whole-vector scales; state and justify the JL dimension for a given \(n\) and \(\varepsilon\), including its independence from \(d\); compute Marchenko–Pastur edges for a given aspect ratio and use them to judge whether an observed spectrum shows real structure; and explain, from variance of a sum, why attention divides by \(\sqrt{d_k}\) and why initialization scales as \(1/\sqrt{\text{fan\_in}}\).

# Calibration, proper scoring rules, and conformal prediction

A model that outputs \(0.8\) is making a claim. This unit is about what that claim means, how to test it, how to score it without rewarding dishonesty, and how to attach a guarantee to a prediction even when the model is badly wrong.

Three separate questions get confused constantly, so separate them now:

- **Calibration** — when the model says \(0.8\), does the event happen \(80\%\) of the time? A property of the *probabilities*.
- **Scoring** — how good is this forecast overall, in a way that cannot be gamed? A property of the *evaluation rule*.
- **Coverage** — can I produce a set of outcomes that contains the truth with a stated probability, with no assumption that the model is correct? A property of a *procedure*.

A model can be perfectly calibrated and useless. A model can be sharp and dangerously overconfident. And a model can be both bad and still support a valid coverage guarantee. Each section below makes one of those statements precise.

## 0. Prerequisite check

You should be comfortable with conditional expectation, the law of total expectation, the idea of a sampling distribution, quantiles of an empirical distribution, and the meaning of a coverage statement from [hypothesis testing and confidence intervals](07-hypothesis-testing-confidence-power.md). Exchangeability, developed for permutation tests in [resampling and experimental design](08-resampling-sequential-experimental-design.md), is the central assumption of section 7.

## 1. What calibration actually claims

Let \(q(X)\in[0,1]\) be a model's predicted probability that \(Y=1\). The model is **perfectly calibrated** when

$$
P\bigl(Y=1\;\big|\;q(X)=p\bigr)=p
\qquad\text{for every }p\text{ in the range of }q .
$$

Equivalently \(E[Y\mid q(X)]=q(X)\): the predicted probability is the conditional mean given itself. This is a statement about a *joint* distribution of \((X,Y)\), not a property the model carries around on its own.

Two immediate observations, both of which people get wrong:

**Calibration is not accuracy.** Predict the base rate \(\bar p\) for every input. Then \(P(Y=1\mid q(X)=\bar p)=\bar p\) exactly, so the model is perfectly calibrated — and it has learned nothing. The missing property is **sharpness**: how far the predictions spread away from the base rate. Calibration without sharpness is worthless, and section 4 makes the tradeoff arithmetic.

**Accuracy is not calibration.** A classifier that outputs \(0.99\) whenever it is right \(90\%\) of the time can have excellent accuracy and terrible probabilities. Any decision that compares a probability to a cost threshold — abstain, escalate, retry, route to a human — breaks under that model even though its top-1 accuracy looks fine.

> **Practice — Foundation:** State in one sentence what a model claims when it outputs \(0.3\), and give an observable consequence of that claim.
>
> **Practice — Core:** Construct a two-input example where model A has higher accuracy and model B is better calibrated, and name a decision rule that prefers each.
>
> **Practice — Stretch:** Show that \(E[Y\mid q(X)]=q(X)\) implies \(E[Y]=E[q(X)]\), and explain why matching average predicted probability to the base rate is necessary but far from sufficient for calibration.

## 2. Reliability diagrams and the trouble with ECE

Calibration conditions on \(q(X)=p\), an event of probability zero for a continuous score. In practice we bin. Partition \([0,1]\) into \(K\) bins, and in bin \(k\) with \(n_k\) observations record the mean predicted probability \(\bar q_k\) and the empirical rate \(o_k\). Plotting \(o_k\) against \(\bar q_k\) gives a **reliability diagram**; perfect calibration is the diagonal.

The usual summary is the **expected calibration error**

$$
\widehat{\mathrm{ECE}}=\sum_{k=1}^K\frac{n_k}n\bigl|\bar q_k-o_k\bigr| .
$$

It is worth knowing exactly how bad this estimator is.

**ECE is biased upward, always.** Even under *perfect* calibration, \(o_k\) is a sample proportion and fluctuates around \(\bar q_k\). Since ECE takes absolute values, those fluctuations cannot cancel — they add. For a bin with \(n_k\) observations near probability \(p\), the mean absolute deviation of a sample proportion is approximately

$$
E\bigl|o_k-p\bigr|\approx\sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}}\cdot\sqrt{\frac{p(1-p)}{n_k}} .
$$

**Worked example — a perfect model with ECE 0.04.** Take a perfectly calibrated model, \(K=10\) bins, \(1000\) observations, so \(n_k=100\), and scores near \(p=0.5\). Then

$$
E|o_k-p|\approx0.798\times\sqrt{\frac{0.25}{100}}=0.798\times0.05\approx0.040 .
$$

Averaging over bins gives \(\widehat{\mathrm{ECE}}\approx0.04\) for a model whose true calibration error is exactly zero. Reporting "our ECE is 0.04, so we are well calibrated" is therefore not a measurement — without a null it is indistinguishable from perfection.

Three consequences to carry:

- **ECE is not comparable across bin counts.** More bins means smaller \(n_k\), which means more upward bias. A model can be made to look better or worse by rebinning alone.
- **ECE is not comparable across sample sizes.** The bias shrinks like \(1/\sqrt{n_k}\).
- **ECE needs a null.** Simulate outcomes from the model's own predicted probabilities, recompute ECE many times, and report the observed value against that reference distribution. This is the same discipline as the permutation nulls in the resampling lesson.

Better options exist — equal-mass rather than equal-width bins, kernel or spline smoothing of \(E[Y\mid q]\), and debiased estimators — but the reporting discipline matters more than the estimator choice.

![A reliability diagram compares predicted probability against observed frequency, while split conformal turns calibration scores into a set with guaranteed coverage.](../assets/calibration-and-coverage.svg)

> **Practice — Foundation:** With \(K=15\) equal-width bins and 3,000 points, compute the approximate ECE floor for a perfectly calibrated model with scores near \(0.5\).
>
> **Practice — Core:** Explain why equal-mass bins change the bias profile, and state what they cost in interpretability.
>
> **Practice — Stretch:** Design a simulation-based null for ECE, state precisely which hypothesis it tests, and explain why it does not test whether the model is *useful*.

## 3. Proper scoring rules: evaluation that cannot be gamed

A scoring rule \(S(q,y)\) assigns a loss to forecast \(q\) when outcome \(y\) is observed. It is **proper** if, whenever the true probability is \(p\), the expected score is minimized by reporting \(q=p\), and **strictly proper** if \(p\) is the unique minimizer. Properness is exactly the statement that *honesty is optimal*.

**The Brier score is strictly proper.** With \(S(q,y)=(q-y)^2\),

$$
E_p\bigl[S(q,Y)\bigr]=p(1-q)^2+(1-p)q^2 .
$$

Differentiating in \(q\),

$$
\frac{d}{dq}E_p[S]= -2p(1-q)+2(1-p)q=2(q-p),
$$

which vanishes only at \(q=p\), and the second derivative is \(2>0\). Reporting anything other than your true belief strictly increases expected loss.

**The log score is strictly proper.** With \(S(q,y)=-[y\log q+(1-y)\log(1-q)]\),

$$
E_p[S(q,Y)]
=-p\log q-(1-p)\log(1-q)
=H(p)+\operatorname{KL}(p\Vert q),
$$

and \(\operatorname{KL}(p\Vert q)\ge0\) with equality only at \(q=p\) by Gibbs' inequality. This is cross-entropy: **the standard training loss is a strictly proper scoring rule**, which is why maximum likelihood and honest probability reporting are the same objective — see [estimation and likelihood](06-estimation-likelihood-fisher.md).

**Accuracy is improper, and that is not a technicality.** Threshold at \(0.5\) and score \(\mathbf1\{\hat y\ne y\}\). Expected loss for report \(q\) is \(p\) if \(q<0.5\) and \(1-p\) if \(q>0.5\): it depends on \(q\) only through which side of the threshold it lands. A forecaster maximizing accuracy is indifferent between reporting \(0.51\) and \(0.99\), and any tie-breaking that rewards confidence pushes reports to the extremes. **Optimizing accuracy actively destroys calibration information.** The same argument applies to any metric computed after an argmax: top-1 accuracy, exact match, pass@1.

The two proper rules differ in what they punish. Log score is unbounded: a confident wrong answer costs infinity, so it punishes overconfidence severely. Brier is bounded by 1, so it is more forgiving of a confident mistake and more sensitive to bulk miscalibration. Choose by the decision you face, and say which you chose.

> **Practice — Foundation:** Compute the Brier and log scores for \(q=0.9\) with \(y=1\) and with \(y=0\).
>
> **Practice — Core:** Prove strict properness of the log score directly from Gibbs' inequality, stating where strictness comes from.
>
> **Practice — Stretch:** A leaderboard ranks models by accuracy. Show that a model can rise on that leaderboard by a transformation that strictly worsens its log score, and propose a reporting rule that prevents this.

## 4. The decomposition: calibration is only one term

For a binned forecast with base rate \(\bar o\), the Brier score decomposes exactly as

$$
\mathrm{BS}
=\underbrace{\sum_k\frac{n_k}n(\bar q_k-o_k)^2}_{\text{reliability (lower better)}}
-\underbrace{\sum_k\frac{n_k}n(o_k-\bar o)^2}_{\text{resolution (higher better)}}
+\underbrace{\bar o(1-\bar o)}_{\text{uncertainty (fixed)}} .
$$

Reliability is calibration error. Resolution is sharpness — how much the outcome rate varies across the groups the model separates. Uncertainty is a property of the data alone and no model can change it.

**Worked example — calibrated versus useful.** Let the base rate be \(\bar o=0.3\), so uncertainty is \(0.3\times0.7=0.21\).

- *Model A* predicts \(0.3\) for everyone. Reliability \(=0\), resolution \(=0\). \(\mathrm{BS}=0.21\).
- *Model B* splits the data in half, predicting \(0.1\) for one half where the rate really is \(0.1\), and \(0.5\) for the other half where the rate really is \(0.5\). Reliability \(=0\), resolution \(=\tfrac12(0.1-0.3)^2+\tfrac12(0.5-0.3)^2=0.04\). \(\mathrm{BS}=0.21-0.04=0.17\).

Both are perfectly calibrated. Only B carries information. **This is why "we improved calibration" is not by itself a result** — a temperature that flattens every prediction toward the base rate improves reliability and destroys resolution. Report both terms, or report a proper score that already combines them.

> **Practice — Foundation:** Compute the three terms for a model that predicts \(0.5\) everywhere when the base rate is \(0.5\).
>
> **Practice — Core:** Construct a model with worse reliability but better Brier score than model B above, and explain how that is possible.
>
> **Practice — Stretch:** Derive the decomposition from the law of total variance applied to \(E[Y\mid q(X)]\), and identify which term each piece corresponds to.

## 5. Recalibration: fixing probabilities without retraining

Miscalibration is often a monotone distortion, which means it can be repaired by a one-dimensional post-hoc map fitted on **held-out** data.

- **Platt scaling** fits \(\sigma(as+b)\) to a score \(s\) by logistic regression: two parameters.
- **Isotonic regression** fits the best nondecreasing map: flexible, but it can overfit small calibration sets and produces a step function.
- **Temperature scaling** divides logits by a single \(T>0\) before the softmax, fitted by minimizing held-out log loss. Because dividing all logits by a positive constant cannot change their order, **temperature scaling leaves argmax predictions and therefore accuracy exactly unchanged**. It only moves the probabilities. \(T>1\) softens an overconfident model; \(T<1\) sharpens an underconfident one.

Two rules that are violated constantly. **Fit the calibration map on data the model did not train on**, or you will simply relearn the training-set overconfidence. And **evaluate calibration on a third split**, because the calibration set is now fitted data.

> **Practice — Foundation:** Explain why temperature scaling cannot change top-1 accuracy.
>
> **Practice — Core:** A model is recalibrated on its training set and reports ECE near zero. Say what has gone wrong and what you would measure instead.
>
> **Practice — Stretch:** Isotonic regression with a 500-point calibration set produces a map with 40 steps. Analyze the variance of this estimator and propose a defensible alternative.

## 6. Calibration does not survive distribution shift

Calibration is a property of the joint distribution of \((X,Y)\). Change the distribution and the property disappears, even with the model untouched.

The cleanest case is **prior shift**: \(P(X\mid Y)\) is unchanged but the class balance moves from \(\pi_{\text{train}}\) to \(\pi_{\text{test}}\). Then the correctly adjusted odds are

$$
\frac{P_{\text{test}}(Y=1\mid x)}{P_{\text{test}}(Y=0\mid x)}
=\frac{P_{\text{train}}(Y=1\mid x)}{P_{\text{train}}(Y=0\mid x)}
\cdot\frac{\pi_{\text{test}}/(1-\pi_{\text{test}})}{\pi_{\text{train}}/(1-\pi_{\text{train}})} .
$$

A model calibrated on a 50/50 training mixture and deployed where the positive rate is \(1\%\) will be wildly overconfident until this correction is applied — and the correction requires knowing the new base rate.

For covariate shift and concept drift there is no such closed form. The practical conclusion is that a calibration claim must name the distribution it was measured on, and that recalibration is an ongoing operation, not a one-time fix. This is the same lesson as the evaluation-under-shift material in [sampling design and ML evaluation](10-sampling-design-ml-evaluation.md).

> **Practice — Foundation:** Apply the prior-shift correction to a predicted probability of \(0.6\) when training prevalence was \(0.5\) and deployment prevalence is \(0.05\).
>
> **Practice — Core:** Derive the odds-ratio formula from Bayes' rule, stating exactly where \(P(X\mid Y)\) invariance is used.
>
> **Practice — Stretch:** Propose a monitoring scheme that detects calibration drift in production using only delayed, partially observed labels, and state its blind spots.

## 7. Conformal prediction: coverage without believing the model

Everything above tries to make the model's probabilities trustworthy. Conformal prediction takes the opposite route: **assume nothing about the model, and still guarantee coverage.**

**Split conformal.** Fit any model on a training split. Take a separate calibration set of \(n\) examples and compute a **nonconformity score** \(s_i=s(X_i,Y_i)\) — any function measuring how badly the model fits that pair. For regression, \(s_i=|Y_i-\hat f(X_i)|\). For classification, \(s_i=1-\hat q(X_i)_{Y_i}\), one minus the probability assigned to the true label. Larger means stranger.

Set

$$
\hat q_\alpha=\text{the }\left\lceil(n+1)(1-\alpha)\right\rceil\text{-th smallest of }s_1,\ldots,s_n ,
$$

and for a new input predict the set

$$
C(X_{n+1})=\bigl\{y:\;s(X_{n+1},y)\le\hat q_\alpha\bigr\} .
$$

**Theorem.** If \((X_1,Y_1),\ldots,(X_{n+1},Y_{n+1})\) are exchangeable, then

$$
P\bigl(Y_{n+1}\in C(X_{n+1})\bigr)\ge1-\alpha ,
$$

and if the scores are almost surely distinct, coverage is also at most \(1-\alpha+\tfrac1{n+1}\).

**Why it is true, in one paragraph.** Exchangeability says all \((n+1)!\) orderings of the scores \(s_1,\ldots,s_{n+1}\) are equally likely, so the **rank** of the test score \(s_{n+1}\) among all \(n+1\) scores is uniform on \(\{1,\ldots,n+1\}\). Hence \(P(s_{n+1}\le s_{(k)})\ge k/(n+1)\) where \(s_{(k)}\) is the \(k\)-th smallest calibration score. Choosing \(k=\lceil(n+1)(1-\alpha)\rceil\) makes that at least \(1-\alpha\). No property of \(\hat f\) is used anywhere — it is a statement about ranks.

**Worked example.** With \(n=1000\) and \(\alpha=0.1\), \(k=\lceil1001\times0.9\rceil=\lceil900.9\rceil=901\), so \(\hat q_\alpha\) is the 901st smallest of the 1000 calibration residuals. Note the requirement \(k\le n\), which forces \(n\ge1/\alpha-1\): at \(\alpha=0.05\) you need at least 19 calibration points, and far more for a stable threshold.

**What the guarantee does and does not say.**

- It is **marginal**, averaged over \(X\). Coverage can be \(99\%\) on easy inputs and \(60\%\) on hard ones while the average hits \(90\%\). Group-conditional (Mondrian) conformal restores coverage within declared groups; exact conditional coverage is impossible without assumptions.
- It says nothing about **set size**. A trivially wide set covers perfectly. Model quality shows up as *efficiency*, not validity — always report average set size alongside coverage.
- It requires **exchangeability**, which fails under temporal drift, clustered data, and any calibration set contaminated by training data. The failure modes are identical to those of the permutation tests in the resampling lesson, for the same reason.
- Every reuse of the calibration set to *select* a model or score function re-enters the selection problem of the hypothesis-testing lesson.

In an LLM setting this is the principled backbone of selective prediction: define a nonconformity score from the model's own confidence, calibrate a threshold, and abstain when the prediction set is too large or does not meet the threshold. The guarantee holds even though the model's own probabilities are untrustworthy.

> **Practice — Foundation:** Compute \(k\) for \(n=500,\alpha=0.05\) and for \(n=50,\alpha=0.01\). Is the second feasible?
>
> **Practice — Core:** Explain why the rank argument needs exchangeability but not independence, and give a dependent-but-exchangeable example.
>
> **Practice — Stretch:** A team calibrates conformal thresholds on data from January and deploys in June with observed coverage of \(78\%\) against a target of \(90\%\). Give three mechanisms, the measurement that distinguishes each, and one adaptive method that would have degraded more gracefully.

## 8. Failure modes

- **Reporting ECE without a null or a bin count.** Both are required for the number to mean anything.
- **Optimizing an improper metric** and then wondering why probabilities are extreme.
- **Calling a flattened model "better calibrated"** when resolution was destroyed.
- **Recalibrating on training data**, or evaluating calibration on the calibration split.
- **Quoting calibration measured on one distribution as if it holds on another.**
- **Presenting conformal coverage without set size**, or using conformal sets under clear drift.
- **Treating a proper score as a complete evaluation.** It measures forecast quality, not utility, fairness, or cost-weighted risk — those need the decision-theoretic machinery of [information, learning, and decisions](../06-information-learning-decision/01-entropy-generalization-decisions.md).

## 9. Runnable labs

**Lab A — expected calibration error.** Implement `expected_calibration_error` in the [learner exercises file](../../labs/exercises.py). Given predicted probabilities, binary outcomes, and a bin count, place each probability into an equal-width bin over \([0,1]\), and return the ECE together with per-bin summaries of count, mean predicted probability, and observed rate. Reject empty input, mismatched lengths, probabilities outside \([0,1]\), outcomes other than 0/1, and non-positive bin counts. Empty bins contribute nothing.

Then investigate: simulate a perfectly calibrated model by drawing \(q_i\sim\mathrm{Uniform}(0,1)\) and \(y_i\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(q_i)\). Compute ECE for \(K\in\{5,10,20,50\}\) at \(n\in\{500,5000,50000\}\) and tabulate the results. Confirm the bias grows with \(K\) and shrinks with \(n\), and compare against the \(\sqrt{2/(\pi n_k)}\cdot\sqrt{p(1-p)}\) prediction.

**Lab B — split conformal threshold.** Implement `conformal_threshold` in the [learner exercises file](../../labs/exercises.py). Given calibration nonconformity scores and a miscoverage level \(\alpha\), return the \(\lceil(n+1)(1-\alpha)\rceil\)-th smallest score. Reject an empty score list, non-finite scores, \(\alpha\) outside \((0,1)\), and any \((n,\alpha)\) pair for which the required rank exceeds \(n\) — in that case no finite threshold can guarantee coverage.

Then investigate: generate calibration and test scores from the same distribution, and estimate empirical coverage over many repetitions. Confirm it lands in \([1-\alpha,\;1-\alpha+1/(n+1)]\). Then make the test scores systematically larger — a stand-in for distribution shift — and measure how fast coverage degrades.

## 10. Derivations to own

1. Strict properness of the Brier score by differentiating the expected loss.
2. Strict properness of the log score via \(E_p[S]=H(p)+\operatorname{KL}(p\Vert q)\).
3. The impropriety of thresholded accuracy, and why it drives reports to the extremes.
4. The reliability–resolution–uncertainty decomposition of the Brier score.
5. The upward bias of ECE under perfect calibration, including the \(\sqrt{2/\pi}\) factor.
6. The prior-shift odds correction from Bayes' rule.
7. The conformal rank argument, from exchangeability to the \(\lceil(n+1)(1-\alpha)\rceil\) quantile.

## 11. End-of-unit practice (graded)

**Foundation**

1. A weather model says \(0.7\) on 200 days and it rains on 130. Is this consistent with calibration? Give a rough check.
2. Compute the Brier and log scores for \(q=0.02\) when \(y=1\). Which rule punishes more, and by how much?
3. For \(n=200\) and \(\alpha=0.1\), give the conformal rank \(k\).

**Core**

4. Decompose the Brier score for a model with base rate \(0.4\) that predicts \(0.2\) on half the data (true rate \(0.25\)) and \(0.6\) on the other half (true rate \(0.55\)). Report all three terms.
5. Show that temperature scaling is a monotone reparameterization of the logits and therefore cannot change any argmax-based metric. Then say precisely which metrics it can change.
6. A model reports ECE \(=0.035\) with \(K=20\) bins on \(n=4000\) points. Estimate the ECE floor for a perfectly calibrated model in that setting and state what you can conclude.
7. Prove that conformal coverage is at least \(1-\alpha\) using only the uniformity of the rank of \(s_{n+1}\).

**Stretch**

8. A team improves ECE from 0.08 to 0.02 by temperature scaling, and downstream task performance falls. Explain how both can be true, name the quantity that moved in the wrong direction, and design the experiment that confirms it.
9. An LLM abstention system uses conformal calibration on a static benchmark and is deployed on live traffic where prompts arrive in bursts from the same users. State which conformal assumption is violated, what direction coverage will move, and give a resampling unit that restores validity.
10. Argue that no scoring rule can simultaneously be strictly proper, bounded, and invariant to the base rate, or give the counterexample. Then say which of the three properties you would give up for a medical triage model and why.

<details><summary>Solution sketches</summary>

1. The observed rate is \(130/200=0.65\) against a claim of \(0.70\). The standard error is \(\sqrt{0.7\times0.3/200}\approx0.032\), so the deviation is about \(1.5\) standard errors — consistent with calibration on this evidence alone.
2. Brier \(=(0.02-1)^2=0.9604\); log score \(=-\log(0.02)\approx3.91\). The log score is unbounded and punishes the confident error far more; Brier cannot exceed 1.
3. \(k=\lceil201\times0.9\rceil=\lceil180.9\rceil=181\).
4. Uncertainty \(=0.4\times0.6=0.24\). Reliability \(=\tfrac12(0.2-0.25)^2+\tfrac12(0.6-0.55)^2=0.0025\). Resolution \(=\tfrac12(0.25-0.4)^2+\tfrac12(0.55-0.4)^2=0.0225\). \(\mathrm{BS}=0.0025-0.0225+0.24=0.22\).
5. Dividing by \(T>0\) preserves the order of logits, so the argmax is fixed: accuracy, top-\(k\), and exact match are unchanged. It changes every probability-dependent quantity: log loss, Brier, ECE, entropy, abstention rates at a fixed threshold, and any expected-cost decision.
6. Per bin, \(n_k=200\); at \(p\approx0.5\) the floor is \(0.798\times\sqrt{0.25/200}\approx0.028\). An observed 0.035 is barely above the floor, so the data do not support a strong calibration claim in either direction; report the simulated null distribution instead.
7. Exchangeability makes the rank of \(s_{n+1}\) uniform on \(\{1,\ldots,n+1\}\), so \(P(\text{rank}\le k)=k/(n+1)\). With \(k=\lceil(n+1)(1-\alpha)\rceil\ge(n+1)(1-\alpha)\), this is at least \(1-\alpha\), and the event \(\{\text{rank}\le k\}\) implies \(s_{n+1}\le s_{(k)}=\hat q_\alpha\).
8. Temperature scaling above 1 flattens predictions, improving reliability while reducing resolution; any threshold-based downstream policy loses separation. Confirm by reporting the decomposition before and after: reliability falls, resolution falls too, and the proper score barely moves or worsens.
9. Bursty repeated prompts from the same users break exchangeability between calibration and test points — the test scores are positively dependent within a burst, so effective sample size is far below \(n\) and realized coverage becomes more variable and typically lower. Calibrate on user-level units, or use a conformal variant with group-level exchangeability.
10. Strict properness plus boundedness is achievable (Brier), but base-rate invariance is not: the uncertainty term \(\bar o(1-\bar o)\) is a fixed component of any proper score, so scores are not comparable across datasets with different prevalence. For triage, give up boundedness and use the log score, because a confident miss should be punished without limit.

</details>

## Mastery check

State what a calibration claim asserts and test it with an appropriate null rather than a bare ECE number; prove properness for Brier and log scores and explain why argmax metrics are improper; decompose a Brier score into reliability, resolution, and uncertainty and use it to reject a "better calibration" claim that destroyed sharpness; correct probabilities for prior shift; and construct a split-conformal predictor from scratch, state its guarantee exactly, name the assumption it rests on, and report coverage together with set size.

title: Latent variables, the ELBO, and gradient estimators
